newsitem.title: ALBANIA: No quick fix for Albania's economic woes-experts.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix for Albania's economic woes-experts.

text.p: Financial analysts say there is no quick fix to ease Albania's economic turmoil and they doubt if hundreds of thousands of small investors will ever get their money back.
The country's biggest investment holding company promised to repay small investors who were panicked by the collapse of a string of get-rich-quick pyramid schemes last month.
But a trader at a Tirana bank said it was unlikely that the company, Vefa Holding, whose interests range from hotels to mines, could find enough cash to repay all of its investors.
"Unless the company gets new loans very soon, they'll go under," he predicted.
Vefa, one of four investment firms which froze client assets after five pyramid schemes failed, offered on Wednesday to pay back those investors who had put less that $5,000 into the company.
The reimbursement of small investors got off to a slow start on Thursday. About 2,000 people crowded outside the headquarters of Vefa, which had previously frozen the accounts of its 80,000 clients.
A senior Western banking source said he doubted if any of the failed pyramid schemes would be able to generate enough cash to repay tens of thousands of impoverished investors.
"A pyramid company cannot, by definition, have enough assets to match liabilities," he told Reuters.

Vefa has steadfastly maintained that it is solvent and has 240 businesses in Albania ranging from beer and tourism to supermarkets and petrol stations. It says it has no relation to pyramids, except that the scandal frightened its investors.
It estimates its total assets at $500 to $600 million. But just covering the small investors, who represent 60 percent of its accounts, could cost the company up to $240 million.
Vefa officials insisted they had received sufficient foreign credits as well as having an array of assets which could be sold to generate cash if necessary.
Pyramid schemes suck in money by offering sky-high interest rates and prosper by paying existing investors with the money of the new. They fail when the flow of new cash dries up.

Economists believe Albanians sank up to $2 billion, about 80 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), into such funds, money that was desperately needed to fund the poor country's economic revival.

The funds, which blossomed after the old communist regime was ousted in 1990, were fuelled by the absence of a functioning banking system and the hordes of cash sent home by hundreds of thousands of Albanians working illegaly abroad.
The government has promised some of the hardest-hit savers that they will be exempt from taxes for two years, but it insists that it will not print money to bail out investors.
The domestic currency, the Lek, has plunged some 25 percent against the dollar this year and signs of economic trouble are obvious across the mountainous Balkan state.

Industrial activity has come to an almost complete standstill. Unemployment in some places tops 80 percent, with those in work scratching a living as waiters or running one of the make-shift kiosks that have sprung up along the pot-holed streets.
The government of President Sali Berisha, elected in 1992 on a free-market ticket, ran a deficit of 10 percent of GDP last year. This year's budget has yet to be agreed upon.
Foreign experts say international financial assistance will be essential to get Albania out of its economic woes.
"The danger of instability exists, but the opportunities for success are just as big," Carlos Elbirt, the World Bank's representative in Albania, told Reuters.
"The key for (ensuring) sustainable growth is creating the necessary physical and institutional infrastructure. A lot more could and should have been done in this respect."
